q: Under NSCP 2015, what are dead loads?
o: The weight of all materials and fixed equipment built into the structure
The weight of occupants and furniture
Loads from wind and earthquake
Loads that act only during construction
n: Dead loads include walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, stairs, finishes, cladding and fixed service equipment such as cranes.

q: Under NSCP 2015, when is a masonry or concrete wall classified as a bearing wall?
o: When it supports any load at all
When it supports more than 2.90 kN/m of vertical load in addition to its own weight
When it supports more than 1.0 kN/m
Only when it is thicker than 200 mm
n: The thresholds are 2.90 kN/m for masonry or concrete walls and 1.45 kN/m for metal or wood stud walls, beyond the wall's own weight.

q: In strength design, what must hold true?
o: The service stresses must not exceed allowable stresses
The deflection must equal the span/360
The factored load effects must not exceed the design strength (φ × nominal strength)
The dead load must exceed the live load
n: Strength design (used for concrete and masonry) factors the loads up and the strengths down, then checks φRn ≥ U.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a garage?
o: Any covered parking area without walls
A shed for tools
A storage room for fuel only
A building or part of one where motor vehicles containing fuel are stored, repaired or kept
n: The definition turns on fuel-carrying vehicles because of the fire and explosion risk, which affects fire separation and loads.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a parapet wall?
o: The part of a wall entirely above the roof line
A wall that carries the roof
A low wall along a stair
A wall between two units
n: Parapets rise above the roof edge. They must be designed for wind and seismic forces as cantilevers, and their bracing is often overlooked.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a prefabricated assembly?
o: Any member cast in place
A structural unit whose parts are assembled before it is placed in the building
A temporary scaffold
A mix of concrete delivered by truck
n: Prefabricated units, such as trusses or precast panels, are built off site or on the ground and then installed as one piece.

q: What is a strength limit state?
o: A limit state of excessive deflection only
A limit state of appearance
A limit state where the structure loses strength or stability and becomes unsafe
A limit state of cost
n: Strength limit states concern safety: yielding, buckling, fracture or overturning. Serviceability limit states concern function, such as deflection and vibration.

q: What does allowable stress design (ASD) require?
o: That factored loads stay below φ times nominal strength
That only dead load is considered
That members never deflect
That stresses computed under service load combinations stay below allowable stresses
n: ASD divides the material strength by a factor of safety to get an allowable stress and checks it against stresses from unfactored (service) loads.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is an awning?
o: A shelter supported entirely from the exterior wall of a building
A roof projecting over public property on columns
An exterior floor on posts
A window hood made of glass only
n: An awning hangs entirely off the building wall. A marquee is a permanent roofed structure projecting over public property.

q: Under NSCP 2015, when is a metal or wood stud wall classified as a bearing wall?
o: When it supports more than 2.90 kN/m
When it supports more than 1.45 kN/m of vertical load in addition to its own weight
When it supports any load at all
Never; only concrete walls can be bearing walls
n: Light stud walls become bearing walls at a lower load, 1.45 kN/m, than masonry or concrete walls (2.90 kN/m).

q: What does load and resistance factor design (LRFD) require?
o: That service stresses stay below allowable stresses
That all members are the same size
That factored loads not exceed the factored resistance, so no limit state is reached
That wind is ignored
n: LRFD applies load factors to the loads and resistance factors to the strengths. It is the steel and wood name for the same idea as strength design in concrete.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a deck?
o: An exterior floor that only projects from the building
A roof with no parapet
A floor inside a building
An exterior floor supported on at least two opposing sides by the structure or by independent posts
n: A deck has its own supports on at least two sides. An exterior balcony projects from the building with no independent supports.

q: Under NSCP 2015, how steep must a wall element be to count as an exterior wall?
o: Sloped at 60° or more from the horizontal
Sloped at 30° or more
Perfectly vertical only
Any slope
n: A wall or element enclosing the outside of the building counts as exterior if it slopes at least 60° to the horizontal. Flatter surfaces are treated as roofs.

q: Which design method name is traditionally used for reinforced concrete and masonry?
o: LRFD
Strength design
Plastic design
Working stress only
n: Concrete and masonry chapters of NSCP call it strength design (USD). Steel and wood call the same idea LRFD.

q: What is a limit state?
o: The maximum height allowed by zoning
The boundary of the lot
A condition beyond which a structure no longer does its job or becomes unsafe
The last day of construction
n: Limit states are grouped into strength (safety) and serviceability (function). Design keeps the structure away from all of them.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a retaining wall?
o: A wall that carries floor loads only
A wall above the roof line
A fire wall
A wall designed to hold back soil or other material
n: Retaining walls resist lateral earth pressure. They are checked for overturning, sliding and bearing as well as for strength.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is an access floor system?
o: Removable panels on pedestals that leave space below for cables, services or air
A floor that is open to the public
A ramp for wheelchairs
A floor of metal grating
n: Access floors are common in data centers and offices. NSCP requires them to carry extra load (a 1.0 kPa allowance) besides the live load.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what do live loads exclude?
o: People
Dead, construction and environmental loads such as wind, rain and earthquake
Movable furniture
Stored goods
n: Live loads come from use and occupancy. Construction loads and environmental loads are treated separately in the load combinations.

q: What is allowable stress design also called?
o: Ultimate strength design
Load and resistance factor design
Working stress design
Plastic design
n: ASD and working stress design mean the same thing: service loads compared with allowable (working) stresses.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is an exterior balcony?
o: An exterior floor on posts at both ends
An interior mezzanine
A roof garden
An exterior floor projecting from and supported by the structure, with no independent supports
n: A balcony is a cantilever from the building. NSCP gives it a higher live load (2.9 kPa for residences) than the floor inside.

q: A reinforced concrete wall carries its own weight plus 2.0 kN/m from the floor above. Under NSCP 2015, is it a bearing wall?
o: No, because 2.0 kN/m is below the 2.90 kN/m threshold for concrete walls
Yes, because it carries some floor load
Yes, because it is concrete
No, because concrete walls can never be bearing walls
n: A masonry or concrete wall becomes a bearing wall only above 2.90 kN/m of vertical load besides its own weight. A stud wall with the same 2.0 kN/m would be a bearing wall, since its threshold is 1.45 kN/m.

q: Which design method name is traditionally used for structural steel and wood?
o: Ultimate strength design
Load and resistance factor design (LRFD)
Working stress only
Plastic hinge design only
n: Steel and wood chapters use LRFD, with ASD as an alternative. Both check the same limit states in different ways.

q: What are essential facilities?
o: Buildings with more than ten storeys
Any government office
Buildings that must stay in use during and after extreme events such as earthquakes and typhoons
Buildings used only for storage
n: Hospitals, fire and police stations and evacuation centers must keep working after disasters, so they get the highest importance factors.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a non-bearing wall?
o: A wall with no windows
A wall under 2 m high
A glass wall only
Any wall that does not meet the definition of a bearing wall
n: Partitions and infill walls below the load thresholds are non-bearing. They still must carry their own weight and resist out-of-plane wind and seismic forces.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a structure?
o: Anything built or constructed, made of parts joined together in a definite manner
Only a building with walls and a roof
Only steel frames
Only structures taller than 10 m
n: The definition is broad and covers towers, tanks, signs and retaining walls as well as buildings.

q: Which of these is a serviceability limit state?
o: Collapse of a column
Excessive deflection or vibration of a floor
Overturning of a wall
Fracture of a tension member
n: Serviceability limit states affect use and comfort (deflection, vibration, cracking) rather than safety.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is an addition?
o: Any repair of finishes
A change of occupancy only
An extension or increase in the floor area or height of a building
A new building on a separate lot
n: Additions add area or height and must meet the code for new work. An alteration changes existing construction or occupancy.

q: Under NSCP 2015, an assembly building gathers at least how many persons?
n: An assembly building gathers 50 or more people for purposes such as worship, entertainment, education, dining or awaiting transportation.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a marquee?
o: A permanent roofed structure attached to a building and projecting over public property
A shelter hung from the exterior wall only
A temporary tent
A sign painted on a wall
n: Marquees extend over sidewalks or other public property, so they are regulated for height, projection and loads.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is an alteration?
o: Only the demolition of a building
Any change, addition or modification in construction or occupancy
Only a new building
Only painting
n: An alteration covers any change to existing construction or use. The altered parts must comply with the code.
